description_full: Erie Indemnity Company operates as a managing attorney-in-fact for the subscribers at the Erie Insurance Exchange in the United States. It provides issuance and renewal services; sales related services, including agent compensation and sales and advertising support services; underwriting services that include underwriting and policy processing; and other services consist of customer services and administrative support services, as well as information technology services. The company was incorporated in 1925 and is based in Erie, Pennsylvania.
ceo_bio: Ms. Julie Marie Pelkowski CPA | Executive VP & CFO | Age 55 | Compensation: $890,927 (FY2025)

financial_summary: Erie Indemnity Company is a large-cap financial services business with a $14.3B market cap on $4.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 7% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $571M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.23× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 45% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 18% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 12pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.68x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 19% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 13% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 0.51, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.21 vs 5y 0.34), so read it loosely.
About $48.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 21% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 47% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $208 (margin of safety -31%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $163 to $279 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/E 24.8 vs 12.2, EV/EBITDA 17.5 vs 10.9 and P/FCF 25.0 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 17% below its 10-year median.
The price implies 6.8% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 7.4% by 19pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.46).
It converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 24% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.7% over 3 years, 9.9% over 5 years and 10.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 23%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 18.9% on average.
Analysts expect 3.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 45.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 46%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (2.1% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 30 consecutive years, though it has been cut 1.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,667 employees, each generates about $610K of revenue, 1.2x the Financial Services median.
That works out to $86K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $891K (1x revenue per employee).
